subject: science
title: US Middle School Science - Evolution and Adaptation
subtitle: Natural selection, inherited variation, adaptations, extinction, and evidence for evolution.
description: Reading passages for a middle school life science pack on evolution and adaptation. Passages emphasize evidence, data, case studies, and scientific reasoning about natural selection.

data.sourcePassage: Evolution is a change in inherited traits of a population over many generations. An individual organism does not evolve during its lifetime. A lizard may grow, learn where to find food, or lose part of its tail, but those changes are not evolution because they are not changes in inherited trait frequencies across generations. Populations evolve when traits passed from parents to offspring become more or less common. If dark mice on a lava field survive predators more often and leave more offspring, dark fur may become more common in that mouse population over time. The key idea is that individuals are born with inherited traits, environments affect which traits are helpful, and reproduction passes those traits to the next generation.

questions.question: What evolves in the scientific definition used here?
questions.modelAnswer: Populations evolve over generations.

questions.question: Why is a lizard losing part of its tail not evolution by itself?
questions.modelAnswer: It is a change to one individual during its lifetime, not a change in inherited traits across a population over generations.

questions.question: How could dark fur become more common in a mouse population on lava rock?
questions.modelAnswer: Dark mice may be harder for predators to see, survive more often, reproduce more, and pass dark fur traits to offspring.

questions.question: Which phrase best shows that the change is evolution?
questions.modelAnswer: Inherited trait frequencies change across generations.
options: One mouse learns a new route
Inherited trait frequencies change across generations

questions.question: Explain why reproduction is necessary for natural selection to change a population.
questions.modelAnswer: Traits become more common only when organisms with those inherited traits leave offspring that inherit them.

data.sourcePassage: Variation means that individuals in a population are not exactly the same. Some birds may have longer beaks, some plants may grow taller, and some bacteria may carry genes that help them survive an antibiotic. Variation can come from mutations and the mixing of genes during reproduction. An adaptation is an inherited trait that helps an organism survive or reproduce in its environment. Adaptations are useful in particular situations, but they are not perfect. Thick fur helps a polar bear stay warm in Arctic conditions, but the same kind of trait could be harmful in a hot environment. A trait that helps in one place may not help somewhere else.

questions.question: What does variation mean?
questions.modelAnswer: Variation means differences in traits among individuals in a population.

questions.question: Name one source of variation from the passage.
questions.modelAnswer: Variation can come from mutations or from the mixing of genes during reproduction.

questions.question: Why are adaptations described as useful in particular situations rather than perfect?
questions.modelAnswer: The usefulness of a trait depends on the environment, so a trait that helps in one setting may be harmful or less useful in another.

questions.question: Which example from the passage is an adaptation?
questions.modelAnswer: Thick fur helping a polar bear stay warm is an adaptation.

questions.question: How does variation make natural selection possible?
questions.modelAnswer: Natural selection needs differences among inherited traits so that some traits can affect survival and reproduction more than others.

data.sourcePassage: Peppered moths in England are a well-known example of natural selection. Before heavy industrial pollution, many tree trunks were light-colored because lichens grew on them. Light-colored moths were harder for birds to see on those trees. During industrial pollution, soot darkened the tree trunks. Dark moths became harder for birds to see, so they had a survival advantage in polluted areas. The moths did not turn dark because they wanted to hide. Variation in moth color already existed. Birds acted as a selective pressure, and the environment changed which color was more helpful. Over generations, the more helpful color became more common.

questions.question: What selective pressure is described in the passage?
questions.modelAnswer: Bird predators were the selective pressure.

questions.question: What happened to tree trunks during industrial pollution?
questions.modelAnswer: Soot darkened the tree trunks.

questions.question: Why did dark moths have an advantage in polluted areas?
questions.modelAnswer: Dark moths were harder for birds to see on soot-darkened trunks, so they were less likely to be eaten and more likely to reproduce.

questions.question: Which statement avoids the misconception in the passage?
questions.modelAnswer: Variation already existed, and the environment favored one color over another.
options: Moths became dark because they wanted to hide
Each moth chose a better color
Variation already existed, and selection favored one color

questions.question: How does this example show that fitness depends on the environment?
questions.modelAnswer: Light moths had an advantage on light trunks, while dark moths had an advantage when soot made trunks dark.

data.sourceTitle: Data from Beetles, Finches, and Bacteria
data.targetTitle: Data from Beetles, Finches, and Bacteria
data.sourcePassage: Data can help scientists explain natural selection. In a beetle model, 34 light beetles and 16 dark beetles survived on light bark, but 13 light beetles and 37 dark beetles survived on dark bark. The pattern suggests that camouflage depended on the background. Finch data showed average beak depth rising from 8.8 millimeters before a drought to 9.7 millimeters after hard seeds became common, then falling to 9.2 millimeters when small seeds returned. In a bacterial model, resistant bacteria increased from 2 percent to 88 percent after repeated antibiotic exposure. In each case, the data matters because it shows a change in survival or trait frequency connected to an environmental pressure.

data.sourcePassage: Scientists use several lines of evidence to understand evolution. Fossils show that different organisms lived at different times in Earth history. In undisturbed rock, deeper layers are usually older than layers above them. Comparative anatomy shows that different species can have similar structures, such as the front limb bone patterns of humans, bats, whales, and cats, even when the limbs have different functions. DNA evidence is especially powerful because species with more similar DNA are usually more closely related. Embryology can show similarities in early development, and direct observations allow scientists to watch populations with short generation times, such as bacteria or insects, change over time. No single source stands alone; the strongest explanations combine many kinds of evidence.

questions.modelAnswer: Fossils use preserved remains or traces of ancient organisms.

questions.question: In undisturbed rock, which layers are usually older?
questions.modelAnswer: Deeper or lower layers are usually older.

questions.question: How can comparative anatomy support common ancestry?
questions.modelAnswer: Similar body structures in different species can suggest that those species inherited related structures from a common ancestor.

questions.question: Why is DNA evidence powerful for comparing species?
questions.modelAnswer: Species with more similar DNA are usually more closely related.
options: Similar DNA can show close relationships

questions.question: Why is it stronger to combine several lines of evidence?
questions.modelAnswer: Combining fossils, anatomy, DNA, embryology, and direct observations gives a more reliable explanation than relying on only one source.
